There used to be noise, you know, the good kind. People trooping in and out. Neighbours, people from our mosque, alfas, children she helped, women she advised, men she encouraged. item.title: Food, Floods, Erosion: 16,140 households targeted with 5,380 tubewells, dams, irrigation projects in Kano
item.description: •Inside the Ecological Project Office interventions in dry-season farming By Nnamdi Ojiego For farmers in Kano State, the end of the rainy season often marks a difficult transition. As rainfall declines, access to water becomes a major concern, particularly for smallholder farmers who depend on seasonal rains to cultivate their land. In communities exposed to flooding and erosion, the challenges are even greater, with damaged roads, threatened homes and disrupted economic activities adding to the difficulties of rural life. In Sumaila Town, Sumaila Local Government, for instance, residents faced serious challenges due to a lack of accessible roads and the threat of gully erosion. Vehicles could not enter parts of the neighbourhood, forcing car owners to park outside. Against this backdrop, the Federal Government has embarked on a series of ecological and agricultural interventions across Kano State, combining flood control, erosion remediation, road improvement and irrigation infrastructure in a programme intended to support farming throughout the year. Ecological interventions The erosion and flood-control component of the programme covers a range of communities where the government has listed projects intended to address erosion, flooding and deteriorating road infrastructure. The project schedule contains 32 entries, including the construction of bridges and culverts for flood control, erosion-control works, remediation of affected areas and road improvement along selected routes. Among the locations listed are Zambur, Unguwar Gai in Kibiya Local Government Area, Rimmin Yamma and Sumaila, Rurum-Bunkini-Kazaurawa, Furuwa, Kibiya town bypass, Zango and Hanyar Kogo in Takai, Kachako, Karaye, Kukar Bashari and Kwanar Dan Goro. Other locations include Fulatan in Rogo Local Government Area, Kadabo Road, Darki bypass in Wudil, Kiru, Tiga-Runum Road, Gala, Wudil town, Daki community, Bebejii, Kadauji village and Magami. The programme also lists road improvement and erosion-control works along Sabon Gwandu, Kazaurewa-Gana Road in Rano, Unguwar Gora, Rano-Bunkure Road and Falali in Sumaila, among other locations. The projects vary in their stated purposes. Some are primarily concerned with erosion control, while others combine erosion remediation with road improvement. Several involve the construction of bridges or culverts intended to help manage flooding and improve movement within affected communities. Such infrastructure can be important in rural areas where roads provide links between farms, residential settlements, markets and other essential services. Where erosion damages roads or floodwaters cut off access, farmers may encounter additional difficulties moving produce to buyers, obtaining agricultural inputs or reaching their fields. The listed interventions therefore have potential implications beyond the physical structures being constructed. Their value to communities will depend on whether they address the problems for which they were designed and whether the infrastructure remains functional after construction. Challenge of flooding, erosion Flooding and erosion can place considerable pressure on communities whose livelihoods depend on agriculture and local trade. Heavy rainfall can wash away topsoil, damage roads, undermine structures and disrupt the movement of people and goods. Where water is poorly channelled, runoff can gradually erode the land, deepen gullies and threaten farmland and residential areas. Flooding can also make roads impassable, leaving some communities with limited access to markets and essential services. For farming households, the effects may extend beyond the immediate damage. The loss of productive land, interruption of cultivation and difficulty transporting harvested crops can affect household earnings and food availability. The Federal Government’s programme addresses some of these concerns through a combination of erosion-control structures, bridges, culverts and road improvement works. The inclusion of bridges and culverts in locations such as Zambur, Furuwa, Magami and Unguwar Gora suggests an effort to address specific points where water movement and access are important considerations. Other projects focus on erosion remediation or the improvement of roads in towns and rural settlements. However, without adequate maintenance, infrastructure intended to control erosion and flooding can deteriorate, reducing its effectiveness over time. The programme’s long-term value will therefore depend not only on construction but also on the quality of the works, their suitability for local conditions and the arrangements for monitoring and maintenance. Irrigation expansion While the erosion and flood-control projects address environmental and infrastructure challenges, the irrigation component seeks to improve access to water for agriculture. The EPO has listed interventions at Tiga, Challawa-Gorge and Kafin Chiri dams, with plans to open new sectors for irrigation and provide canal networks to serve designated areas of farmland. Together, the three schemes are designed to cover 1,279.91 hectares. The Tiga Dam intervention accounts for 875 hectares, Challawa-Gorge for 240 hectares and Kafin Chiri for 164.91 hectares. The proposed schemes combine main canals, distribution canals, field canals and pipe extensions, depending on the requirements of each location. The objective, according to the documents, was to make water available for cultivation beyond the main rainy season, giving farmers an opportunity to grow crops during periods when rainfall alone may not support production. Dry-season farming can provide an additional source of income for farmers and help maintain agricultural activity when rain-fed cultivation is no longer possible. Depending on local conditions, crops grown under irrigation can also supply markets at different times of the year. For the intervention to achieve these aims, however, the infrastructure must be completed, supplied with adequate water and operated in a way that allows farmers to use it reliably. Tiga Dam: 875 hectares earmarked for irrigation The Tiga Dam scheme is the largest of the three irrigation interventions listed in the project material. Completed in 1974, Tiga Dam is a major water-storage structure associated with the Kano River Irrigation Project. The supplied technical data describes it as a zoned earth-fill dam with a length of 6,000 metres and a maximum height of 48 metres from foundation level.

item.title: INEC Figures: How North-West, South-West may hold key to Aso Rock
item.description: •Candidates’ performance in two regions has shaped presidential election since 1999 By Luminous Jannamike Behind the battle for the presidency lies a contest over voter numbers, party machinery and political alliances. Tinubu has a head start as incumbent, but Atiku, Obi and other challengers know that no region is anybody’s political inheritance. The road to Aso Rock in 2027 runs through two regions where elections can be won, lost or thrown wide open: the North-West and South-West. Their combined electoral strength gives them enormous influence over the calculations of President Bola Tinubu and the opposition figures seeking to unseat him. The Independent National Electoral Commission’s 2026 voter register puts the North-West at 25,083,411 registered voters and the South-West at 19,614,274. Together, they account for 44,697,685 registered voters, representing more than 43 per cent of Nigeria’s 103,428,715 registered voters ahead of the 2027 general elections. Those figures make the two zones central to the presidential contest. But the real battle is more complicated than regional arithmetic. Candidates must convert registered voters into ballots, hold their traditional strongholds, penetrate rival territories and build a coalition broad enough to survive the country’s political and geographical divisions. For Tinubu, the stakes are particularly high. His South-West political base helped launch his presidential ambition, while his 2023 victory also depended on support beyond the region. Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi must find ways to disrupt that balance if they hope to deny him a second term. The numbers that can make or break a candidate The North-West’s 25.08 million registered voters make it Nigeria’s largest geopolitical voting bloc. The South-West follows with 19.61 million, ahead of the North-Central, which has 16.97 million. The political significance is unmistakable. Kano, Kaduna and Katsina are among the country’s most populous electoral states, while Lagos leads the national register with 7,488,633 voters. A candidate who makes substantial gains across these states can dramatically improve his national tally. Yet neither zone is a political inheritance. The North-West contains competing party structures, influential local leaders and voters whose choices are shaped by security, economic conditions, personalities and the performance of elected officials. Lagos demonstrated this in 2023 when Obi defeated Tinubu there by 9,848 votes, polling 582,454 against the president’s 572,606. The South-West follows with 19.61 million, ahead of the North-Central, which has 16.97 million. The political significance is unmistakable. Kano, Kaduna and Katsina are among the country’s most populous electoral states, while Lagos leads the national register with 7,488,633 voters. A candidate who makes substantial gains across these states can dramatically improve his national tally. Yet neither zone is a political inheritance. The North-West contains competing party structures, influential local leaders and voters whose choices are shaped by security, economic conditions, personalities and the performance of elected officials. Kano’s political history, in particular, shows how a powerful state-level movement can disrupt calculations made in Abuja. The South-West presents a different challenge. Tinubu’s longstanding political network gives him an advantage, but it does not guarantee uniform support across the region. Lagos demonstrated this in 2023 when Obi defeated Tinubu there by 9,848 votes, polling 582,454 against the president’s 572,606. That result remains a reminder that even a candidate’s home territory can become a battleground. Party loyalty, local grievances, urban voting patterns and the credibility of candidates can all upset expectations. The numbers also require caution. INEC’s register measures people registered to vote, not the number who will eventually cast ballots. Turnout, voter accreditation, election-day logistics and the distribution of votes among candidates will determine how much of that numerical advantage translates into electoral power. What elections since 1999 reveal Nigeria’s presidential elections have repeatedly shown that regional strength matters most when it forms part of a wider national coalition. Olusegun Obasanjo’s victories in 1999 and 2003 rested on support extending beyond his South-West origins. Umaru Musa Yar’Adua’s 2007 victory reflected the strength of the Peoples Democratic Party’s national machinery, while Goodluck Jonathan’s 2011 success drew on substantial support in the South and parts of the North. The 2015 election changed the political landscape. Muhammadu Buhari’s victory demonstrated that an opposition alliance could defeat an incumbent when it combined a formidable northern base with support in other parts of the country. The merger that produced the All Progressives Congress brought together political interests that had previously competed against one another. Buhari’s re-election in 2019 again showed the importance of maintaining a broad electoral coalition, even as the contest exposed persistent regional divisions. Pate cautioned that this similarity did not, by itself, establish a direct epidemiological link between the two patients or explain precisely how the infection reached Nigeria. Authorities must establish whether anyone else has been infected, while ensuring that hospitals can recognise and safely manage any suspected cases that emerge. Second responsibility That second responsibility is particularly important. A patient with fever, headache, vomiting or diarrhoea may have any of several illnesses. But when the symptoms are accompanied by a relevant exposure history, health workers must know what questions to ask, whom to notify and how to protect themselves and others while the patient is assessed. An outbreak may be detected by a laboratory, but preventing further transmission also depends on what happens at the patient’s first point of contact with the health system. item.title: Some people in Tinubu’s administration don’t want Fashola – Ex-presidential aide
item.description: Former presidential aide Laolu Akande has alleged that some individuals close to President Bola Tinubu opposed the appointment of the former Minister of Works and Housing Babatunde Fashola to the current administration. In an interview on the Naija Unfiltered podcast, published by Symfoni TV on Friday, Akande attributed Fashola’s absence from the Federal Government partly to possible fatigue on his part but said resistance from people within the President’s circle was a more significant reason. “I think the reason why Fashola is not in this government, two reasons. I think Fashola himself has a bit of fatigue; more importantly, I think there are people around the president who don’t want to see Fashola because Fashola is not going to tolerate many of those things that you are seeing around,” Akande said. He described the former minister as someone who stands firmly by his principles and would not compromise to accommodate practices he considers unacceptable. “Whatever you say about Fashola, he doesn’t take nonsense and the people who wanted to get some nonsense going, they didn’t want Fashola,” he said. Akande did not disclose the identities of the individuals he accused of opposing Fashola’s inclusion in the administration. He also failed to provide specific examples of the alleged practices they wanted to protect. Fashola was Lagos State governor from 2007 to 2015 before joining the cabinet of former President Muhammadu Buhari. Akande maintained that the former governor remained close to President Tinubu despite his non-inclusion in the administration. “Even somebody like Fashola, who is still very close to the president, no problems openly,” he said. The former presidential aide also questioned whether Tinubu was making sufficient use of capable individuals who could challenge his decisions when necessary. He argued that effective governance required people who could disagree with the President when they believed his decisions or the actions of those around him were wrong. Akande cited Fashola as an example of a politician who would stand his ground, alleging that some individuals within Tinubu’s circle preferred not to have such a figure in the administration. item.title: Blaming opposition for hunger is delusional — Atiku
item.description: By Luminous Jannamike & Olayinka Ajayi Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar has accused President Bola Tinubu of shifting responsibility for Nigeria’s economic hardship to the opposition, insisting that the administration must account for its record ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Read Also: 2027: ‘They created the hunger’ — Tinubu slams opponents at Kaduna rally Atiku, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), was reacting to Tinubu’s remark at the APC campaign flag-off in Kaduna on Saturday that the opposition created hunger and poverty in the country. In a statement issued by his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku described the President’s comment as “either delusion or a staggering case of political amnesia”. “The APC governed Nigeria for eight years before you took office. You have added another three and a half years. Nigerians know who has been in power, and hardship did not begin when the opposition started talking about it. Stop insulting their intelligence and answer for your record,” he said. Atiku accused Tinubu’s administration of worsening the hardship faced by Nigerians, arguing that the President could not dismiss concerns about the cost of living by blaming political opponents. He also criticised Tinubu’s planned inauguration of a section of the Abuja-Kaduna Expressway, alleging that the ceremony showed how disconnected the President was from the daily realities of Nigerians. “A road cannot be completed with a speech or a ribbon cutting ceremony,” he said. The former Vice President challenged the administration to explain the removal of the petrol subsidy and the depreciation of the naira, which he claimed had fallen from about ₦471 to ₦1,329 to the dollar. He also cited a World Bank estimate that 63 per cent of Nigerians would be below the national poverty line in 2026, accusing the government of presiding over rising poverty. Atiku further questioned the extension of the 2024 budget into 2025 alongside a separate 2025 budget, as well as what he described as ₦7.13 trillion recorded under “energy security” in 2024 and ₦11.2 trillion in NNPC pipeline-related spending. item.title: CHI Farms, Aviagen celebrate 20-year partnership
item.description: CHI Farms Limited, a member of Tropical General Investments (TGI) Group, is celebrating 20 years of partnership with Aviagen, a global poultry breeding company behind the Arbor Acres® brand, to support poultry farmers across Nigeria. The partnership has provided farmers with access to quality breeding stock, advanced genetics and technical expertise to improve productivity and flock performance. Over the years, the collaboration has expanded to include farmer training, knowledge sharing and technical support tailored to local production conditions, contributing to the growth of Nigeria’s poultry industry. Commenting on the milestone, Dr Olatunji Olaitan Olaofe, Managing Director of CHI Farms, said the anniversary reflected the company’s commitment to delivering value to customers. He expressed appreciation to Aviagen for its support and to customers for their continued trust in the company. Florian Blevin, Business Manager, Sub-Saharan Africa, Aviagen, commended CHI Farms for its longstanding commitment to the Nigerian poultry industry and its role in making Arbor Acres genetics accessible to local producers. Both companies reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the partnership and supporting a more productive and sustainable poultry industry in Nigeria. item.title: How Echono is driving quiet revolution at TETFund
item.description: By Kennedy Elaigwu Awodi For decades, the public conversation surrounding Nigeria’s tertiary education sector was dominated by systemic deficits, inadequate physical infrastructure, underfunded laboratories, brain drain, and recurring industrial friction. While interventionist agencies like the Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund) were established to bridge these gaps, early approaches often leaned heavily on physical construction, brick, mortar, and concrete, at the expense of commercializable research, technological innovation, and modern academic governance. However, a fundamental structural evolution is underway. At the epicenter of this transformation is Arc. Sunday “Sonny” Echono, the Executive Secretary of TETFund. A seasoned public administrator and former President of the Nigerian Institute of Architects, Echono brought an architect’s structural precision and a career bureaucrat’s institutional depth when he assumed leadership of the agency in March 2022. Under his stewardship, TETFund is evolving from a traditional funding mechanism into a dynamic engine of institutional modernization, applied research, and economic self-reliance. Historically, public tertiary institutions suffered from a critical disconnect: academic research often ended up stacked on dusty library shelves, failing to translate into viable real-world products or market solutions. Arc. Echono identified this challenge early on, shifting TETFund’s strategic emphasis toward Research for Impact (R4I) and technology commercialization. Through targeted initiatives, such as launching innovation hubs across tertiary institutions in the six geopolitical zones and rolling out state-of-the-art multipurpose laboratories, TETFund is creating physical and intellectual sandboxes for Nigerian academics. These spaces allow scholars, innovators, and students to prototype solutions addressing pressing national challenges in agriculture, renewable energy, cybersecurity, and public health. By fostering entrepreneurship within academia, Echono is helping build a higher education model that creates job opportunities and drives national economic productivity. Through targeted initiatives, such as launching innovation hubs across tertiary institutions in the six geopolitical zones and rolling out state-of-the-art multipurpose laboratories, TETFund is creating physical and intellectual sandboxes for Nigerian academics. Still in hysterics, I made a run for the office. I felt really good Before he came back, I’d already taken time off to move my things. For me, revenge wasn’t sweet – it was pepperish!” Rele’s experience reminded me of what happened to another friend years ago when her husband dumped her after 14 years of marriage and two kids. “Was that it after all the year we’d been together? Hurt and a sense of being betrayed conjures different emotions that might result in the aggrieved concocting different forms of revenge. It is seldom worth it as after a while you wonder how you could be capable of such atrocities. Giving yourself time to mourn is the best revenge. It gives you the freedom to plan for a better relationship. How To Enjoy The Things You Like Without Feeling Guilty Some of the most ‘saintly’ assumptions about your health could play havoc with your well-being. Here’s why new findings believe you should drop the good-girl act and have fun keeping healthy: You’ve cut out sweets and chocolate:- If you’re trying to lose weight, not eating chocolate and other sweet food is a good idea but putting them on a list of food no-no can seriously backfire and ruin your weight-loss efforts. The reason? Deprive yourself of something and you’re more likely to binge. In fact, researchers have found that successful dieters who lost weight and kept it off, didn’t bank any food and allowed themselves regular treats. Instead:- The key is to limit your intake to small amount and fulfil your urge by opting for truly decadent options – a small slice of super-rich chocolate cake is much more satisfying than lots of tasteless biscuits. You rarely miss a day at the Gym:- If you think never taking a breather from your work-out makes you ultra-healthy, you’re mistaken. Obviously being inactive isn’t a good idea, but exercising can lead to muscle aches and tears, joint injuries, low energy levels, extreme tiredness, decreased immunity and even depressing, so it’s essential to give yourself time off. But that’s not all – exercising every day can prevent you from getting the results you deserve. It’s while your body is resting that it repairs muscle cells and syntheses new enzymes, mitochondria and capillaries, which makes you fitter. In other words, if you don’t give yourself a break, your fitness abilities won’t progress. Instead:- Exercise for a maximum of five days a week. And don’t worry about taking small work-out breaks – research shows that going for up to seven days without breaking a sweat won’t impact your fitness significantly. Your body fat is below 18 per cent:- Not having enough body fat can be dangerous. Fat insulates nerve cells and internal organs and is necessary for the formation of hormones such as oestrogen. When body fat dips too low, you go into famine mode, which effectively shuts down all non-life-supporting functions such as ovulation and building new bone. item.title: Clashes Break Out In Paris, Other French Cities Amid Fresh Protests
item.description: Clashes broke out Saturday in Paris and other French cities amid demonstrations held a week after others that degenerated into street violence and prompted a robust security backlash as President Emmanuel Macron seeks to restore order. Police arrested nearly 1,000 people as officers were confronted with “an extremely elevated level of violence” from black-clad “ultra-left” extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. Riot squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes. They created hunger, they created poverty, we are trying to eradicate it,” he said. “We pay salaries regularly, our governors are working, I am proud of them, they are developing.
